📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, CISA has added three newly introduced vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-131914 Idunno AntiCsrf Deserialization of Untrusted Data Vulnerability  CVE-2026-132165 Drupal Core Remote Code Execution Vulnerability  CVE-2026-132224 Optimizely Web Experimentation External Control of Critical State Data Vulnerability  These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria. Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

Introducing the llama.cpp benchmark dashboard for AMD Ryzen and Radeon

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (389 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the llama.cpp × AMD Benchmark dashboard is available on Hugging Face.
  • It has been revealed that local inference performance changes as models, kernels, and builds evolve.
  • You can choose Hardware, Model, and llama.cpp build in the Configuration sidebar.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the llama.cpp × AMD Benchmark dashboard is available on Hugging Face. It lets you track prompt processing and text generation performance across llama.cpp builds, models, and quantizations, so you can explore how local inference performs on AMD Ryzen and Radeon hardware.

It has been revealed that local inference performance changes as models, kernels, and builds evolve. We want those changes to be easy to inspect for any AMD developer: pick a hardware, a model and a build, compare quantizations, and follow performance over time. The benchmark workflow and underlying results are public, so you can also inspect how we benchmark inference performance.

You can choose Hardware, Model, and llama.cpp build in the Configuration sidebar. The current hardware choices are Radeon 8060S (gfx1151) and Radeon AI Pro R9700S (gfx1201).

The dashboard shows two separate tests, both measured in tokens per second:.

In a recent development, both tests start at context depth zero (n_depth=0). PP512 measures processing 512 input tokens without generation; TG128 measures generating 128 tokens without a pre-existing context. The plotted value is the mean throughput (avg_ts). These are useful reference workloads, while the Context scaling tab lets you explore token generation throughput as the context grows.

According to recent reports, we benchmark the prebuilt binaries distributed through llama-install.sh, the build and installation project behind llama.app. The public gfx1151 and gfx1201 workflows are scheduled weekly and run the standard benchmarks using the llama-bench tool with Flash Attention on and off, with 10 repetitions per configuration.

Industry observers note that the model set evolves and right now includes Inkling 2 Mini, Qwen, Gemma, gpt-oss, and LFM models, covering both dense and mixture-of-experts architectures. Available GGUF formats include Q4_K_M, Q8_0, other quantizations, and higher-precision formats such as BF16 and F16.

The explorer reads directly from the public ggml-org/install.sh-benches-data Storage Bucket on Hugging Face. The data source link beside the chart title opens the folder for the selected build, hardware, and model.

Standard results use ///.jsonl. Workload sweeps use the same folder -tg.jsonl filename.

Use them to investigate a result, make your own charts, or compare with a local run.

Thanks to the AMD team for providing test infrastructure and helping validate the setup! Try the dashboard, inspect the data, and let us know which models and workloads you would like to see next.
